newsitem.title: POLAND: SOLIDARITY IN NATIONAL PROTEST FOR GDANSK SHIPYARD.
newsitem.headline: SOLIDARITY IN NATIONAL PROTEST FOR GDANSK SHIPYARD.

text.p: Poland's Solidarity union on Tuesday launched nationwide protests to defend the bankrupt Gdansk shipyard from final dismemberment, while the government said it was trying to save at least part of it.

"We announce the conduct by the Solidarity union of an all-Poland protest action, from today until it is revoked, in defence of the Gdansk Shipyard and other workplaces," union leader Marian Krzaklewski told a news conference in Gdansk.
He declined to say exactly what the campaign would consist of but union officials have said it might involve brief stoppages at various plants and street protests.
"Solidarity does not plan to organise a nationwide general strike, but we don't rule out that if confrontation were to mount, one might be possible in defence of the union," he said.

The Baltic coast yard where Solidarity arose in defiance of communist rule in 1980 has been bankrupt since August 1996 and the receiver this month said he would dismiss the last 3,800 workers and sell off the assets, after banks refused credits to build five ships for a German owner.

The right-leaning union accuses the government, led by ex-communists, of failing to aid the yard or at least encourage banks to grant credits for the contracts which could have kept the yard going until an investor appeared.
Krzaklewski said all the union's regional branches would have to appoint special teams to coordinate protest actions in major provincial towns, to be subsidised out of strike funds.
At the same time the union will be collecting money to bail out the yard by selling contribution coupons.
He said the protests might be ended once some conditions were met: "When there are orders (for the yard), when there are banks giving finance and guarantees from the state treasury."

In Warsaw, Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz met heads of the successful Szczecin shipyard, the Polish merchant navy and several ministers, saying he planned to hunt for ways to keep some business going at the Gdansk yard.

The government's spokeswoman Aleksandra Jakubowska said the prime minister would present the conclusions of the meeting to parliament on Thursday. She declined to give details of any possible last-minute rescue package.
Solidarity says the ruling ex-communists have deliberately brought the yard to its knees. The union also demanding more state help for other troubled industries, notably armaments.
The government says the 60-percent state-owned yard's collapse is due to mistakes by its former Solidarity-backed managements and that it cannot risk taxpayer's money to help.

The fate of the enterprise which came to symbolise the democracy struggle leading to the 1989 fall of communism is arousing strong emotions and rallying opposition forces before parliamentary elections due around September this year.

The union has steered dozens of small right-leaning groups into a Solidarity Election Action (AWS) grouping which is now running about level in opinion polls with the ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD).
In Gdansk itself, shipyard workers held a small quiet rally on Tuesday after several days of turbulent protests in which thousands blocked streets and hurled eggs at banks which refused credit.
But local union leaders promised a protest outside the SLD's Gdansk headquarters for Wednesday. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
